US media cited unnamed officials as saying Tehran had privately acknowledged to President Donald Trump's advisers that the shooting at ships was a mistake, though the Iranians reportedly pinned the blame on a rogue internal group. Trump has said both sides have agreed to continue talks despite this week's fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, which the White House saw as a violation of the ceasefire. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said his country had "kept its word" on the ceasefire, saying on X the US had violated the deal.
Vice-President JD Vance is among US officials expected to take part in negotiations resuming on Saturday in Oman.

How Iran's new regime is very different to what came before In June, the US and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement where Iran would, in part, give safe passage to commercial ships. Tehran said that an "errant" sect of hardliners was trying to undermine negotiations by firing on the commercial ships, senior US officials told CBS News, the BBC's US partner. One official told the TV network: "They [the Iranians] came back to the table and said, 'We screwed up. We made a mistake. Let's keep talking.'" Araqchi is also expected to attend the talks.

US media cited unnamed officials as saying Tehran had privately acknowledged to President Donald Trump's advisers that the shooting at ships was a mistake, though the Iranians reportedly pinned the blame on a rogue internal group.

Trump has said both sides have agreed to continue talks despite this week's fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, which the White House saw as a violation of the ceasefire.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said his country had "kept its word" on the ceasefire, saying on X the US had violated the deal.

How Iran's new regime is very different to what came before

In June, the US and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement where Iran would, in part, give safe passage to commercial ships.

Tehran said that an "errant" sect of hardliners was trying to undermine negotiations by firing on the commercial ships, senior US officials told CBS News, the BBC's US partner.

One official told the TV network: "They [the Iranians] came back to the table and said, 'We screwed up. We made a mistake. Let's keep talking.'"

Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and two people who have been heavily involved in Middle East talks - special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner - are expected to lead Saturday's negotiations.

Araqchi is also expected to attend the talks.

In a briefing for reporters on Friday, the US officials said a message to Tehran's leadership had been conveyed through regional mediators demanding Iran release a statement declaring the strait open and that it will stop shooting at commercial ships, according to multiple media reports.

"They're either going to give us that statement or we're not having a good outcome for them," said one official, quoted by Reuters news agency.

The White House also wants Iran to publicly acknowledge that firing on the shipping was a mistake, CBS reports.

Meanwhile, a delegation from Qatar travelled to Iran on Friday for talks aimed at defusing tensions and easing navigation through the Strait of Hormuz.

The US has demanded that Iran publicly declare the Strait of Hormuz open and guarantee maritime security before key Oman talks. But if Tehran has already admitted the recent ship attacks were a mistake, why is Washington still turning up the pressure?

The Strait of Hormuz is once again at the heart of rising US-Iran tensions, with Washington demanding Iran publicly guarantee maritime security before talks begin. If Iran has nothing to hide, why won't it make that promise in public? If Iran admits it was a mistake, why won't it say so publicly?

US officials say President Donald Trump's administration has sent a clear message through regional mediators: Iran must publicly declare that the Strait of Hormuz is open for international shipping and promise to stop targeting commercial vessels.

The US President Trump wrote "The Islamic Republic of Iran has asked us to continue 'talks.' "We have agreed to do so, but the United States has stated to them, in no uncertain terms, that the Cease Fire is OVER!"

The pressure follows June's ceasefire agreement, under which Iran pledged safe passage for commercial ships. But after three vessels were attacked along a US-backed shipping route, confidence in the deal quickly began to fade.

Is this a peace deal or just another pause before the next confrontation?

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi says Tehran has honored the ceasefire and argues that the attacks were carried out by an "errant" hardline group acting on its own. Washington, however, wants more than explanations it wants a public guarantee that such incidents will not happen again.

Saturday's Oman talks are expected to bring together Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Araqchi, making them one of the most significant rounds of US-Iran diplomacy in months.

Adding to the tension, President Trump warned that any threat against him would be met with overwhelming US military retaliation, raising the stakes even before negotiations begin.

The consequences reach far beyond Washington and Tehran. Any instability in the Strait of Hormuz could disrupt global oil supplies, unsettle financial markets, and threaten maritime security across one of the world's busiest trade routes.

payload.title: Yhdysvallat vaatii Iranilta lupausta lopettaa kauppa-alusten tulittaminen Hormuzinsalmessa
payload.summary: Yhdysvallat haluaa Iranin vakuuttavan julkisesti, että Hormuzinsalmi on avoinna, ja sitoutuvan lopettamaan kauppa-alusten tulittamisen. Korkean tason neuvottelujen on määrä jatkua lauantaina Omanissa.
payload.content:
Yhdysvallat vaatii Irania ilmoittamaan julkisesti Hormuzinsalmen olevan avoinna ja sitoutumaan siihen, ettei kauppa-aluksia enää tuliteta. Vaatimuksia on määrä käsitellä lauantaina Omanissa jatkuvissa neuvotteluissa, joihin odotetaan korkean tason edustajia kummastakin maasta tämän viikon taisteluista huolimatta.

## Osapuolet kiistelevät aselevon rikkomisesta

Yhdysvallat ja Iran solmivat kesäkuussa aseleposopimuksen, jonka mukaan Iranin oli muun muassa taattava kauppa-aluksille turvallinen kulku. Valkoinen talo on pitänyt tämän viikon yhteenottoja Hormuzinsalmessa aselevon rikkomisena. Presidentti Donald Trump on kuitenkin sanonut, että molemmat osapuolet ovat sopineet neuvottelujen jatkamisesta.

Yhdysvaltalaismediat ovat nimettömiin viranomaisiin vedoten kertoneet Iranin myöntäneen yksityisesti Trumpin neuvonantajille, että alusten tulittaminen oli virhe. CBS Newsille puhuneiden yhdysvaltalaisviranomaisten mukaan Teheran selitti tulitusten olleen neuvotteluja horjuttamaan pyrkineen kovan linjan sisäisen ryhmän toimintaa. Yksi viranomaisista kuvasi Iranin palanneen neuvottelupöytään ja myöntäneen tehneensä virheen.

Iranin ulkoministeri Abbas Araqchi on puolestaan kiistänyt maansa rikkoneen aselepoa. Hän kirjoitti viestipalvelu X:ssä Iranin pitäneen sanansa ja syytti Yhdysvaltoja sopimuksen rikkomisesta. Osapuolten julkiset näkemykset vastuusta ovat siten ristiriidassa keskenään ennen Omanin tapaamista.

## Omaniin kokoontuu korkean tason valtuuskunta

Yhdysvaltain varapresidentin JD Vancen ja ulkoministeri Marco Rubion odotetaan johtavan lauantain neuvotteluja yhdessä erityislähettiläs Steve Witkoffin ja Trumpin vävyn Jared Kushnerin kanssa. Witkoff ja Kushner ovat osallistuneet tiiviisti Lähi-itää koskeviin neuvotteluihin. Iranin edustajaksi odotetaan ulkoministeri Araqchia. Kokoonpano tekee tapaamisesta yhden viime kuukausien merkittävimmistä Yhdysvaltojen ja Iranin välisistä neuvottelukierroksista.

Trump on lisäksi varoittanut, että kaikki häneen kohdistuvat uhkaukset johtaisivat Yhdysvaltojen voimakkaaseen sotilaalliseen vastaukseen. Neuvottelujen välittömänä aiheena on silti Hormuzinsalmen avaamista ja kauppa-alusten turvallisuutta koskeva sitoumus. Salmen epävakaus voi häiritä maailman öljytoimituksia, horjuttaa rahoitusmarkkinoita ja vaarantaa merenkulun turvallisuutta yhdellä maailman vilkkaimmista kauppareiteistä. Neuvottelut ovat kasvaneista jännitteistä huolimatta yhä toteutumassa.
summary_bullets: Yhdysvallat vaatii Iranilta julkista vakuutusta Hormuzinsalmen avoimuudesta ja kauppa-alusten tulittamisen lopettamisesta.
Neuvottelujen on määrä jatkua lauantaina Omanissa korkean tason valtuuskuntien kesken.
Washington ja Teheran syyttävät toisiaan kesäkuussa solmitun aselevon rikkomisesta.
payload.journalist_note: Artikkeli erottaa osapuolten julkiset kannat nimettömiin yhdysvaltalaisviranomaisiin perustuviin tietoihin. Iranin väitetty yksityinen virheen myöntäminen esitetään siksi välillisenä ja vahvistamattomana tietona.

article.source_text:
Fire blazes in Iran after "powerful" US strikes The US wants Iran to publicly state that the Strait of Hormuz is open and to pledge to stop firing on commercial ships as part of negotiations due to be held in Oman on Saturday. US media cited unnamed officials as saying Tehran had privately acknowledged to President Donald Trump's advisers that the shooting at ships was a mistake, though the Iranians reportedly pinned the blame on a rogue internal group. Trump has said both sides have agreed to continue talks despite this week's fighting over the Strait of Hormuz, which the White House saw as a violation of the ceasefire. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said his country had "kept its word" on the ceasefire, saying on X the US had violated the deal.

Vice-President JD Vance is among US officials expected to take part in negotiations resuming on Saturday in Oman.

How Iran's new regime is very different to what came before In June, the US and Iran signed a ceasefire agreement where Iran would, in part, give safe passage to commercial ships. Tehran said that an "errant" sect of hardliners was trying to undermine negotiations by firing on the commercial ships, senior US officials told CBS News, the BBC's US partner. One official told the TV network: "They [the Iranians] came back to the table and said, 'We screwed up. We made a mistake. Let's keep talking.'" Vice-President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and two people who have been heavily involved in Middle East talks - special envoy Steve Witkoff and Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner - are expected to lead Saturday's negotiations. Araqchi is also expected to attend the talks.

Saturday's Oman talks are expected to bring together Vice President JD Vance, Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Special Envoy Steve Witkoff, Jared Kushner, and Araqchi, making them one of the most significant rounds of US-Iran diplomacy in months. Adding to the tension, President Trump warned that any threat against him would be met with overwhelming US military retaliation, raising the stakes even before negotiations begin. Can trust return when every round of diplomacy starts with another ultimatum? The consequences reach far beyond Washington and Tehran. Any instability in the Strait of Hormuz could disrupt global oil supplies, unsettle financial markets, and threaten maritime security across one of the world's busiest trade routes.
